sections.h2: The shortest path to a sale in Long Branch
sections.html:
The quickest route skips the lender's appraisal and the repair list: a buyer who pays cash and accepts the property as it stands. An agent listing also works in this shore city, though the city's own inspection step, described below, adds days to any sale that transfers title.

Line up these pieces before you accept an offer, since they are what most often slows a Long Branch closing.

  • Property tax paid through the current quarter, with a printout from the tax office.
  • Sewer charges paid to the current quarter at the Long Branch Sewerage Authority.
  • A sign-off from the Building Department that no construction permits are open.
  • Smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and a fire extinguisher that meet the city's rules.

Long Branch sits on the Monmouth County shoreline with 5.12 square miles of land and 1.16 of water. Neighborhood names buyers use include Pier Village and the oceanfront, Downtown, Uptown, the North End, West End, Elberon, Branchport, Hollywood, Kensington Park and Pleasure Bay.

Elberon has its own train stop, and the main Long Branch station sits three blocks from the beach on NJ Transit's North Jersey Coast Line. Route 36 and Route 71 are the main highways. Local NJ Transit buses 831 and 837 run in the city, and Academy Bus serves New York City on its Route 36 and Shore Points lines.

A buyer's inspector will look hard at roofs, siding, windows and basements for the wear that salt air and storm water cause. Precipitation averages about 52.5 inches a year, and winters bring nor'easters.

Hurricane Sandy struck on October 29, 2012, and flooding occurred in Long Branch even though the city avoided the worst of the surge. If your house took water then, keep repair records and any elevation or flood insurance paperwork, because buyers ask for them.

Renters are the majority in this growing city, which is why small investors and landlords are common sellers. The 2020 census counted 14,944 housing units with 17.1 percent vacant, so a fair number of houses and apartments sit empty at any given time.

Population was 33,321 in the 2025 estimate, 5.3 percent above April 2020. Owners occupy 42.5 percent of homes, a typical owner-occupied home is valued at $574,000, and typical rent is $1,876 a month. The city counts 13,140 households, and the average commute is 29.6 minutes.

sections.h2: Compliance certificates required before a sale closes
sections.html:
The Fire Marshal's office issues the Residential Certificate of Compliance under city ordinance 262-25. For a one- or two-family home, a Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm and Portable Fire Extinguisher certificate is required on a change of occupancy or transfer of title, and the compliance certificate itself is required before a change of occupancy.

Long Branch residential compliance fees and rules
Certificate or ruleFee or requirement
Smoke, CO alarm and extinguisher certificate$35.00
Residential Certificate of Compliance$60.00
Both, one- or two-family home$95.00 total
Application validity30 days, including one re-inspection
DeliveryIn person only, original forms

An inspector will not inspect a unit while it is occupied, so plan the inspection for the vacant window between tenants or after you move out.

sections.h2: Selling a Long Branch house as-is
sections.html:
The Fire Marshal publishes a Letter of Intent for Purchase of a Building in As-Is Condition. The buyer circles 30, 60 or 90 days to make repairs, accepts responsibility for permits, and agrees that nobody occupies the building until the Fire Prevention Bureau inspects it and issues a Certificate of Compliance.

That form is useful if your house has deferred maintenance. It lets a cash buyer close first and complete the repairs afterward, while still satisfying the city.

Rentals changed in 2026. Ordinance 16-26, adopted July 22, 2026, amends section 262-25 to require that rentals of one- to four-family dwellings run a minimum of 60 days, so weekend and short-stay rentals no longer fit. Investors planning short stays should read it before buying.

Once you accept an offer, book the Fire Marshal inspection first, since the city does not inspect occupied units and the application is valid for a limited window. Then collect the tax printout, the sewer payoff from the Sewerage Authority and the Building Department's open-permit form. Hand the originals to the city in person, because copies and mailed forms are not accepted.

At the closing table the closing agent records the deed with the Monmouth County Clerk, deducts the state transfer fee from your side and collects the GIT/REP form. A cash buyer removes the loan appraisal from the schedule, but the city's certificates still gate occupancy, so many cash buyers in Long Branch sign the as-is letter and finish repairs afterward.

Tell the buyer early. The compliance application asks for the type of occupancy (rental, sale or owner re-occupy), requires every lease to be attached, and lists the prospective occupants. Occupant names can be changed only within two weeks of the inspection date, after which a new application must be filed.

Because the inspector will not enter an occupied unit, a seller with a tenant in place usually has to wait until the lease ends or negotiate a move-out date. A buyer who plans to keep the tenant may prefer to complete the as-is letter and handle the certificate after closing. Either way, agree on the sequence in the contract so no one is surprised by a $95 fee or a missed appointment.

Installments come due at the start of February, May, August and November. The collector allows ten days before interest runs, records the day a payment arrives instead of its postmark, and wants the block and lot written on every payment. Checks go in a secure box at 344 Broadway, or you can pay online.

Monmouth County follows an alternate assessment calendar, so the appeal deadline is January 15 rather than April 1. The Monmouth County Board of Taxation answers at 732-431-7404. Owners who live in the home may also qualify for the state's property tax reimbursement (senior freeze) and homestead rebate programs.

The seller also pays the state's transfer fee when the closing agent records the deed, and the agent collects a GIT/REP form. Out-of-state sellers prepay estimated income tax of no less than two percent of the price. The Monmouth County Clerk charges $40 for page one of a deed and $10 for every page after it.

faqs.q: What do the Long Branch compliance certificates cost?
faqs.a: The residential certificate is $60 and the smoke, carbon monoxide and extinguisher certificate is $35, for $95 together on a one- or two-family home. Fees are payable to the City of Long Branch.

faqs.q: Do I need open permits closed before selling in Long Branch?
faqs.a: Yes for the compliance application, which needs a Building Department form stating there are no open construction permits on the property.

faqs.q: Can I rent my Long Branch house for a weekend?
faqs.a: No. Ordinance 16-26, adopted July 22, 2026, requires rentals of one- to four-family dwellings to run at least 60 days.

faqs.q: By what date must a Long Branch tax appeal be filed?
faqs.a: By January 15, because Monmouth County runs an alternate assessment calendar. Call the county board of taxation to confirm before you file.

faqs.q: My Long Branch house needs major work. Can I still sell?
faqs.a: Yes. Use the city's as-is letter of intent so the buyer takes 30, 60 or 90 days to complete repairs, and the Certificate of Compliance is issued before anyone occupies the house.
